records.originEnglish: Oil, which alludes to wisdom—the clear knowledge and recognition that “I am your God”—comes after proper eating, suitably directed toward God, to sustain one’s soul. Such eating then adds wisdom and knowledge of God. By contrast, gross eating like an animal dulls the heart and mind. This is like their saying in Bava Kamma: “The reason I did not tell you ... was that I had not eaten ox meat.”
records.themeTitle: Proper nourishment can deepen knowledge of God
records.themeSummary: After describing preparation and sanctification, Et HaOchel concludes with oil as clear recognition of God. The meal’s effect on understanding depends on the way and purpose for which a person eats.

records.targetEnglish: This also has relevance to weekday food, as they said in Bava Kamma: “The reason I did not tell you last evening was that I had not eaten ox meat.” They said in the Mekhilta at the beginning of Beshalach: “Torah was given only to those who ate manna.” This means the bread eaten by ministering angels, which contains exceedingly great spiritual vitality; through it one merits many words of Torah. Presumably all Torah scholars who engage in the Torah given to them are eaters of manna, as it is written: “Whoever accepts the yoke of Torah has the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly occupation removed from him.” His livelihood resembles manna, and certainly contains that holiness which brings into the heart vitality from the truth of the blessed God. Through this one apprehends words of Torah from the truth of His blessed wisdom.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains why the food cited at the end of Et HaOchel can affect understanding. Nourishment can carry spiritual vitality into the heart, making it receptive to Torah; manna is the clearest model of that process. The qualification in Et HaOchel remains decisive: this is the effect of properly directed nourishment, while eating driven by appetite can dull the same faculties.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Receiving Torah’s renewal through the life carried by food
records.reverseThemeSummary: The siman follows daily renewal in Creation, Torah, and prayer into the special reception of Shabbat. It then explains nourishment as a means by which spiritual vitality and Torah understanding enter the heart.
records.reverseExplanation: Et HaOchel adds the distinction between nourishment directed toward sustaining life for God and animal-like overeating. records.originEnglish: The desire for eating and the desire for sexual intercourse are sisters. Wherever you find a boundary against sexual transgression, holiness is mentioned; see the second chapter of Yevamot and the Jerusalem Talmud there, halakhah four. One leads to the other, as it is written in Berakhot: “A full belly produces bad kinds [of conduct]”; in Sotah: “Wine does much”; in Pesachim: “Do not become intoxicated, and you will not sin”; and in Kiddushin: “One who does this eats this,” for it is all one. Sexual relations are also called eating: “Except the bread that he ate”; “She eats and wipes her mouth”; and in the Sages’ words in Ketubot: “She eats with him on Shabbat nights.” At the beginning of Sotah they say: “One who sees a sotah in her disgrace should abstain from wine.” This means that when a person sees the corruption of this desire, he should set his heart to consider the corruption of its companion as well, to set a boundary against it and abstain. It is said: “They sold the boy for a prostitute, and sold the girl for wine,” for the two arise from one another. At the end of Gittin, a fly in a dish is compared to a sotah; see there.

records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel reads the instruction to abstain from wine after seeing a sotah as an inquiry into connected desires. The observer should examine the appetite that can feed the failure he has seen.

records.targetEnglish: For satiety from the desire for eating without holiness draws sin after it, as they said in Berakhot: “A full belly produces bad kinds [of conduct],” and as it is said: “Lest you eat and be satisfied ... and your heart become proud and you forget.” This is “Take care” in eating and satisfaction, that they be in holiness; otherwise the heart will thereby be led astray of itself. [As is known concerning the inward meaning of eating: when one does not raise the sparks in the food, they may, God forbid, corrupt him and cause him to sin.] “And you turn aside,” and so forth. This is explicit in Rashi’s explanation at that place in the Torah.
records.explanation: Divrei Chalomot makes the causal concern explicit: satisfaction without holiness can draw the heart into a further failure without a new, deliberate decision at each step. This explains why Et HaOchel tells an observer of sexual corruption to examine the connected appetite for food and wine. The dream passage is presented as Rav Tzadok’s interpretation of the verse, with its own condition of eating without holiness.

records.reverseThemeTitle: The warning after satisfaction concerns how the heart is drawn away
records.reverseThemeSummary: In a remembered dream interpretation, Rav Tzadok reads the proximity of eating, satisfaction, and the warning against being led astray. The decisive distinction is whether satisfaction is received in holiness.
records.reverseExplanation: Et HaOchel specifies the related appetites behind the dream’s concern: food and wine can feed sexual desire. Its interpretation of the sotah-and-nazirite instruction turns the warning into practical reflection on an appetite that can prepare the way for another failure.

records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel reads the instruction to abstain from wine after seeing a sotah as an inquiry into connected desires. The observer should examine the appetite that can feed the failure he has seen.
records.targetHebrew: וזה, הרואה סוטה בקלקולה יזיר עצמו מן היין, היינו שאם אדם רואה לפי מצב עבודתו שאין ביכולתו לקבל את הדבר הזה לתוכו ולהגביר עליו, וירא פן ימנע אותו מעבודת השי"ת, אז הוא העצה להזיר עצמו מהם שלא יקבלם. והגם שאיתא בש"ס (שבת עז:) לא ברא הקב"ה דבר אחד לבטלה, והיכן הוא הכבוד שמים היוצא מן הדבר הזה. ורק זה בעצמו מה שהאדם אוסר עצמו על זמן ויש לו עבודה בזה, זה הוא בעצמו הכבוד שמים היוצא מהדבר הזה. ולזה כתיב אחר כל הפרשה של הנזיר, ואחר ישתה הנזיר יין, שהשי"ת מבטיח לאדם שלאחר הזמן וסדר עבודתו שיהיה לו יאיר לו השי"ת, איך שיכול לקבל לתוכו ויסייעהו לעבודת השי"ת.
records.targetEnglish: This is “One who sees a sotah in her disgrace should abstain from wine.” If a person sees that, at the present state of his service, he cannot take this thing into himself and prevail over it, and fears that it may prevent him from serving the blessed God, the counsel is to abstain from these things and not receive them. Yet they said in Shabbat: “The Holy One, blessed be He, did not create even one thing without purpose.” Where, then, is the glory of Heaven that comes from this thing? The very fact that the person forbids it to himself for a time and has work to do through this is itself the glory of Heaven that comes from it. Therefore, after the entire passage about the nazirite, it is written: “Afterward the nazirite may drink wine.” The blessed God promises the person that, after this period and the ordered service he will perform, He will illuminate for him how he can receive it into himself and how it will assist his service of the blessed God.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef interprets the same sotah-and-wine instruction through an honest assessment of present capacity. Abstention is productive service when the person cannot yet receive a permitted pleasure without being diverted by it. Its later return to wine explains why Et HaOchel’s boundary addresses the appetite’s current disorder, rather than making the created thing itself purposeless.

records.originHebrew: וְתִקּוּן תַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה קוֹדֶמֶת אֶל הָאָדָם, שֶׁהִיא הַקַּלָּה גַּם כֵּן קְצָת אֶצְלוֹ, וּמִמֶּנָּה יִמָּשֵׁךְ אֶל תִּקּוּן תַּאֲוָה הַשְּׁנִיָּה; וּלְכָךְ הִקְדִּימוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מַסֶּכֶת נָזִיר לְמַסֶּכֶת סוֹטָה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּצַּד הַשְּׁלֵמוּת, שְׁלֵמוּת בַּתַּאֲוָה הַשְּׁנִיָּה הוּא בְּמַעֲלָה יוֹתֵר, שֶׁכֵּן עָנְשָׁהּ גַּם כֵּן יַתִּיר, מִסְּתָמָא גַּם מַעֲלַת תִּקּוּנָהּ עָצוּם, וּלְכָךְ בַּתּוֹרָה קָדְמָה פָּרָשַׁת סוֹטָה לְפָרָשַׁת נָזִיר כְּפִי הַמַּעֲלָה; וַחֲכָמִים הָפְכוּ הַסֵּדֶר כְּפִי סֵדֶר הָאֱנוֹשִׁי בְּהַגָּעָתוֹ אֶל הַמַּעֲלָה.
records.originEnglish: Repairing the desire for eating comes first for a person, since it is also somewhat easier for him; from it he proceeds to repairing the second desire. Therefore our Sages placed tractate Nazir before tractate Sotah. In terms of perfection, perfection regarding the second desire is higher: its punishment too is greater, so presumably the excellence of its repair is immense. Accordingly, in the Torah the passage of the sotah precedes the passage of the nazirite, following their rank. The Sages reversed the order to follow the human sequence of reaching that excellence.
records.themeTitle: The order of growth differs from the ranking of attainments
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel distinguishes the higher attainment from the earlier, more accessible work. The order of the tractates follows human progress from restraint in eating toward the more difficult domain.
records.targetHebrew: וְאָמְרוּ שָׁם: ״מְנָא יָדְעָה?״ (בְּרָכוֹת י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) כִּי קְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית מִדְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּצִנְעָה שֶׁאֵין נִיכָּר וְחַד אָמַר: ״שֶׁלֹּא רָאֲתָה זְבוּב עַל שֻׁלְחָנוֹ״ הַיְינוּ שֶׁהִכִּירָה בַּאֲכִילָתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּתַאֲוַת הַיֵּצֶר הַנִּמְשָׁל לִזְבוּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם ס״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳) וּמִזֶּה יָדְעָה שֶׁגָּדוּר בַּעֲרָיוֹת גַּם כֵּן וְחַד אָמַר: ״סָדִין שֶׁל פִּשְׁתָּן הִצִּיעָה לוֹ, וְלֹא רָאֲתָה קֶרִי עָלָיו״ אַף שֶׁטּוֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ מֵבִיא לִידֵי קֶרִי גַּם לַחֲסִידִים פְּעָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳) וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְהִזָּהֵר בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יֶאֱרַע רַק מַה שֶּׁשּׁוֹמְרִין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁמַּקְדִּישׁ עַצְמוֹ מִלְּמַטָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (ל״ט עַמּוּד א׳) וּמִי שֶׁמִּתְקַדֵּשׁ לְמַטָּה בְּתַכְלִית כֹּחַ הָאֱנוֹשִׁי, כֵּן מְקַדְּשִׁין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה בְּתַכְלִית כֹּחַ הָאֱלֹהִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שִׁיעוּר וְנִיצּוֹל גַּם מִטֻּמְאוֹת הַמּוּכְרָחוֹת בְּטֶבַע הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:
records.targetEnglish: They asked there, “How did she know?” (Berakhot 10b), for the holiness of the covenant is a private matter and is not visible. One said, “She did not see a fly upon his table.” That is, she recognized that his eating did not arise from the desire of the inclination, which is compared to a fly, as is taught there on 61a. From this she knew that he also maintained the boundary against forbidden sexual relations. Another said, “She spread a linen sheet for him and saw no seminal emission upon it.” Although the strain of travel can sometimes bring about such an emission even in pious people, as is taught in Shabbat 127b, this is something a person cannot prevent through his own effort. He is protected from above according to the extent to which he sanctifies himself below, as is taught in Yoma 39a. Someone who sanctifies himself below to the utmost of human capacity is likewise sanctified from above to the utmost of Divine power, which has no measure, and is saved even from impurities that the nature of this world would otherwise necessitate.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim separates the observable refinement of eating from the hidden purity recognized through Elisha’s protection. The latter includes a condition that human effort alone cannot always prevent, and is described as sanctification from above following sanctification below. This helps explain Et HaOchel’s distinction between an accessible starting point and a greater attainment, while preserving the limit of voluntary control.

records.originHebrew: הָעֵצָה הַשְּׁנִיָּה: הַמְּתִינוּת; כִּי יְסוֹד תֹּקֶף הַתַּאֲוָה הַמְּהִירוּת, שֶׁרוֹצֶה לִבְלֹעַ וּלְהַשְׁלִים תַּאֲוָתוֹ חִישׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּבֵיצָה [כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳]: נְטִיעָה מְקַטַּעַת רַגְלֵיהֶן דְּקַצָּבַיָּא וּדְבוֹעֲלֵי נִדּוֹת, שֶׁהֵם שְׁתֵּי תַּאֲווֹת הָרָאשִׁיּוֹת הַנִּזְכָּרוֹת הַבָּאִים מִמְּהִירוּת.
records.originEnglish: The second counsel is deliberation, for the foundation of the force of desire is haste: a person wants to swallow and fulfill his desire quickly. As it is written in Beitzah: “A planting undercuts the excuses of butchers and of those who have intercourse with menstruating women.” These are the two principal desires mentioned above, which come from haste.
records.themeTitle: Deliberation interrupts the rush to satisfy appetite
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel identifies the urge to complete enjoyment immediately as a source of desire’s force. Preparing and entering into a meal gives the person a way to resist being carried by that rush.
records.targetHebrew: כי רק האביון שמחוסר כל כאשר נזדמן לו דבר שחשקה נפשו אינו יכול לצמצם ולעצור א"ע מלחטוף אותה אצלו בחפזו כי מתירא אולי לא יהיה אח"כ לאל ידו להשיגה אבל מי שבטוח ברוב הינו ורכושו יכול שפיר לעצור עצמו ולהמתין בכל הטובות כדי שישיג אותם אח"כ ביתר שאת.
records.targetEnglish: Only the destitute person, who lacks everything, cannot restrain himself from snatching a desired thing hastily when it happens to become available, for he fears that afterward it may no longer be within his power to obtain it. But someone secure in his abundant wealth and possessions can restrain himself and wait for every good thing, so that he will obtain it afterward in greater measure.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim identifies the fear beneath grasping haste: the person fears that the desired good will disappear. Its contrasting image of secure possession explains how inner confidence permits waiting. This gives a psychological account of the deliberation Et HaOchel prescribes, while the rest of Et HaOchel’s paragraph separately distinguishes quick eating that is incidental to established Torah study.

records.originHebrew: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּעֵירוּבִין (נ״ד עַמּוּד א׳): "חֲטֹף וֶאֱכוֹל וְכוּלֵי", נִרְאֶה כִּי יֵשׁ חִלּוּקִים בִּבְנֵי אָדָם, שֶׁמִּי שֶׁכְּבָר אָדוּק וְדָבוּק בְּמַחְשְׁבוֹתָיו בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, אָז יִהְיֶה חוֹטֵף וְאוֹכֵל, דֻּגְמַת בֵּי הִלּוּלֵי שֶׁהַמְכֻוָּן עִנְיָן אַחֵר שֶׁעָסוּק בְּשִׂמְחָתוֹ, רַק בֵּין כָּךְ חוֹטֵף וְאוֹכֵל, מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם מֵיחוּשׁ וַחֲשָׁד כְּלָל לְתַאֲוֹת לְבָבוֹ, וּבָטוּחַ בָּהֶם שֶׁדְּבוּקִים רַק בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה.
records.originEnglish: As for what is written in Eruvin, “Snatch and eat,” and so forth, it appears that there are differences among people. Someone already firmly attached in his thoughts to words of Torah may then snatch and eat, like someone at a wedding whose purpose lies elsewhere and who is occupied with its joy, only snatching something to eat in the meantime. There is no room for concern or suspicion about the desires of his heart, for he is secure that they are attached only to words of Torah and service.
records.themeTitle: Incidental quick eating differs from haste driven by appetite
records.themeSummary: The paragraph’s exception depends on an established attachment of thought and desire to Torah and service. The meal is incidental to that occupation, rather than the object toward which the person rushes.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ אֲכִילַת אוֹתוֹ צַדִּיק — רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, דִּכְפִי דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י דְּאָכַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר נִרְאֶה כְּמִלֵּי כְּרֵיסֵיהּ, אֲבָל הָיָה מִקָּדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם, וְזֶהוּ הַפֶּתַח לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּהַכֹּל לְרָצוֹן לִפְנֵי ה׳ וְעַל כֵּן לֹא רָצָה לְהַנִּיחַ לַאֲחֵרִים יְגִיעוֹ, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַב לְרַב הוּנָא [עֵירוּבִין נד רע״א] ״אִם יֵשׁ לְךָ הֵיטֵב לְךָ״ וְגוֹ׳, ״וְאִם תֹּאמַר אַנִּיחַ לְבָנַי״ כו׳ — כִּי מֵאַחַר דְּבָטוּחַ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁכָּל הֲנָאוֹתָיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, לָמָּה לֵיהּ לְהַנִּיחַ לַאֲחֵרִים שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ מַה יִּהְיוּ
records.targetEnglish: This is the eating of that righteous man, Reish Lakish. According to Rashi’s account that he ate whatever he earned, it appears to be filling his belly; yet it was from the holy things of Heaven. This is what he expounded for himself: everything was for acceptance before God. He therefore did not wish to leave his earnings to others, just as Rav said to Rav Huna in Eruvin: “If you have, benefit yourself,” and so forth, “and if you say, I shall leave it for my children,” and so forth. Since he was secure within himself that all his enjoyments were in holiness, why should he leave them to others whose future character he did not know?
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin gives another carefully conditioned reading of the same Eruvin counsel. Outward consumption does not by itself establish indulgence: Reish Lakish’s conduct is explained through his certainty that the enjoyment serves holiness. This illuminates the condition on Et HaOchel’s exception, without turning that exceptional certainty into a presumption available to every eater.

records.originHebrew: לְהַעֲלוֹת כָּל מַאֲכָלִים מִצּוֹמֵחַ הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הָאֱמוּנָה לְבַד בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְעַל יְדֵי הַבְּרָכָה מִקֹּדֶם שֶׁמַּאֲמִין שֶׁ"לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ"; וּלְכָךְ "אֱמוּנַת" — זֶה סֵדֶר זְרָעִים, וְנִקְבְּעָה מַסֶּכֶת בְּרָכוֹת בִּתְחִלָּתָהּ; וְזֶהוּ הַסֵּדֶר שֶׁל הַעֲלָאַת כָּל מִינֵי הַזְּרָעִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי קִיּוּם הַמִּצְוֹת הַכְּתוּבוֹת בָּהֶם וְהַבְּרָכָה מִקֹּדֶם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָאֱמוּנָה שֶׁהַכֹּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, בֶּאֱמוּנָה הַפְּשׁוּטָה הַקְּבוּעָה בְּלֵב כָּל אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשַׁבָּת [צ״ז עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁהֵם "מַאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים", וּלְכָךְ הוּתַר אֲפִילּוּ לְעַם הָאָרֶץ. אֲבָל אֲכִילַת בָּשָׂר אָסוּר, רַק לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם; וְלָכֵן נִקְבְּעָה מַסֶּכֶת חֻלִּין בְּסֵדֶר קָדָשִׁים, דְּלֹא הוּתַר אֶלָּא לְמִי שֶׁאוֹכֵל חֻלִּין עַל טָהֳרַת קֹדֶשׁ, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁשֻּׁלְחָנוֹ דּוֹמֶה לַמִּזְבֵּחַ, וְהַבָּשָׂר שֶׁאוֹכֵל כְּקָרְבָּן וּבְשַׂר קֹדֶשׁ. וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: מִשֶּׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ אֵין לוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה; וּכְשֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה שֻׁלְחָנוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה, אָז הוּא נַעֲשָׂה דֻּגְמַת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וּמִזְבֵּחַ, וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא אוֹכֵל הוּא דֻּגְמַת כֹּהֲנִים, "כִּי קָא זָכוּ — מִשֻּׁלְחַן גָּבוֹהַּ קָא זָכוּ"; שֶׁהַחֵלֶב וְהַדָּם, רָצָה לוֹמַר עִקַּר הַחִיּוּת שֶׁבַּמַּאֲכָל וְהַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּאָדָם לוֹ, הוּעֲלָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה (שֶׁנִּמְשְׁלוּ לְאֵשׁ שֶׁהוּא אֵשׁ הַמַּעֲרָכָה), שֶׁמַּכִּיר עַל יָדוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן הַחִיּוּת בַּמַּאֲכָל, וְהַנּוֹתֵן הַתַּאֲוָה לָאָדָם וְהַחֵשֶׁק לְזֶה הַמַּאֲכָל לְקַיֵּם נַפְשׁוֹ.
records.originEnglish: Raising all foods that come from plants is accomplished through faith in the blessed God alone, and through the blessing beforehand, by which one believes that “the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord.” Therefore “faith” refers to the order Zeraim, and tractate Berakhot was placed at its beginning. This is the order of raising all kinds of seeds to the blessed God through the fulfillment of their prescribed commandments and the blessing beforehand: the faith that everything belongs to the blessed God. This simple faith is fixed in the heart of every Israelite, as the Sages said in Shabbat that they are “believers, children of believers.” Such food was therefore permitted even to an unlearned person. Eating meat, however, is forbidden except to a Torah scholar. Tractate Chullin was therefore placed in the order Kodashim: it was permitted only to someone who eats ordinary food in the purity of holiness, whose table resembles an altar and whose meat is like an offering and sacred meat. This comes only through words of Torah, as it is written: “Since the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has only the four cubits of halakhah.” When one’s table becomes four cubits of halakhah, it resembles the Temple and altar, and what one eats resembles the priests’ eating: “When they receive their share, they receive it from the table of the Most High.” The fat and blood—that is, the principal vitality within the food and the person’s desire for it—have been raised to the blessed God through words of Torah, which are compared to fire, the fire of the altar’s arrangement. Through them one recognizes that the blessed God gives vitality to the food and gives the person desire and longing for this food to sustain his soul.
records.themeTitle: Faith and Torah raise different forms of nourishment
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel distinguishes plant food raised through basic faith and its mitzvot from meat requiring the table to become a place of Torah. The altar image concerns the direction given to both the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire.
records.targetHebrew: וְעַם הָאָרֶץ אָסוּר, כִּי יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת נִשְׁקָע וְלִהְיוֹת "מָצָא מִין אֶת מִינוֹ וְנִיעוֹר". אֲבָל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְנוּקֶּה בְּחַדְרֵי לִבּוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּבָר יֵשׁ לוֹ יִתְרוֹן עַל הַבְּהֵמָה מִצַּד חָכְמָתוֹ. וְלָכֵן עַל יְדֵי מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא מוֹצִיא כֹּחַ אוֹתָהּ נֶפֶשׁ מֵהִתְלַבְּשׁוּתָהּ בְּנֶפֶשׁ בַּהֲמִית וְכֹחַ בְּהֵמָה. וְכֵן בַּפּוֹעַל, הֲרֵי מִתְהַפֵּךְ בְּשַׂר הַבְּהֵמָה לְהָזִין גּוּפוֹ וְלִהְיוֹת נַעֲשָׂה בְּשַׂר אָדָם, כָּךְ בַּכֹּחַ מִתְהַפֵּךְ כֹּחַ בַּהֲמִי לְכֹחַ אָדָם. וְזֶה טַעַם מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר: "בְּחָכְמָה אִתְבְּרִירוּ", וְהַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם יָכוֹל לְבָרֵר וּלְתַקֵּן נְפָשׁוֹת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא אֵין מְנוּקֶּה לְגַמְרֵי מֵאוֹתָן דְּבָרִים; רַק אִם נַפְשׁוֹ מְשׁוּקַּעַת בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, עַל יְדֵי הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הוּא מַעֲלֶה וּמְתַקֵּן כָּל מִינֵי מַחְשְׁבוֹת זָרוֹת.  אֲבָל עַם הָאָרֶץ מוּתָּר רַק בְּצוֹמֵחַ, כִּי הַבַּעַל חַי יֵשׁ לוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרָכוֹת (סא.), מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן צוֹמֵחַ: הַנְּפָשׁוֹת הַמִּתְלַבְּשׁוֹת בָּהֶם הֵם שֶׁאֵין מִתְלַבְּשִׁים בְּמַחְשְׁבוֹת וּרְצוֹנוֹת דְּרַע שֶׁלָּהֶם, רַק בַּלְּבוּשׁ הַחִיצוֹן דְּמַעֲשִׂים רָעִים, שֶׁהַמַּעֲשֶׂה הַגּוּפָנִית נַעֲשָׂה גַּם כֵּן לְבוּשׁ דְּנֶפֶשׁ רָעָה לְהַלְבִּישׁ נִיצוֹץ נֶפֶשׁ הַקְּדוֹשָׁה, וְאִינּוּן מַזִּיקֵי עָלְמָא כַּנּוֹדָע, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹמוֹ. וְהֵן הֵם הַמִּתְלַבְּשִׁים בַּצּוֹמְחִים גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי הָאֲוִיר, וְאֵין בְּכֹחָם לִפְעוֹל בָּאָדָם הִרְהוּרִים בַּלֵּב וּמוֹחַ, רַק בְּכֹחוֹת הַפְּעֻלָּה. וּבָזֶה "רֵיקָנִין שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כֵּן מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כָּרִמּוֹן" (כִּמְאַמְרָם שָׁם נז.) בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, וְעַל יְדֵי מִצְוֹת מַעֲשִׂיּוֹת שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה בְּכֹחַ הָאֲכִילָה הַהוּא אַחַר כָּךְ הֵם נִתְקָנִים.
records.targetEnglish: An unlearned person is forbidden, for he may become submerged, so that “one kind finds its own kind and is awakened.” A Torah scholar, however, even if he is not cleansed in the chambers of his heart, nevertheless already has an advantage over the animal through his wisdom. Through his thought in words of Torah he therefore brings the power of that soul out of its clothing in an animal soul and animal power. Just as, in actuality, the animal’s flesh is transformed to nourish his body and become human flesh, so, in its power, animal power is transformed into human power. This is the meaning of the Zohar’s statement, “They are clarified through wisdom.” A Torah scholar can clarify and repair souls even though he is not wholly cleansed of those things himself. Provided that his soul is immersed in words of Torah, through those words he raises and repairs all kinds of foreign thoughts. An unlearned person, however, is permitted only plant food, for an animal has an evil inclination, as it is written in Berakhot, whereas a plant does not. The souls clothed in plants are not clothed in their evil thoughts and desires, but only in the outward clothing of evil deeds. The bodily act also becomes a garment of an evil soul, clothing a spark of a holy soul; these are the harmful forces of the world, as is known, and this is not the place for it. These are also clothed in plants through the air. They have no power to produce thoughts in a person’s heart and mind, but only in the powers of action. In this domain, “Even the empty ones of Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate,” in deed; through the practical mitzvot performed afterward with the strength of that eating, they are repaired.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the difference underlying Et HaOchel’s two routes. Animal nourishment involves desire and thought, so Torah’s wisdom must turn its power toward the human purpose; plant nourishment is addressed through practical mitzvot. The passage also qualifies the scholar’s level: it does not require an already perfected heart, but it does require actual immersion in Torah. This gives precise content to the table’s “four cubits of halakhah.”

records.reverseThemeTitle: Torah’s wisdom can transform the power received from food
records.reverseThemeSummary: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the scholar’s eating through the transformation of animal power into human power. Its account distinguishes repair through thought in Torah from the practical mitzvot associated with plant food.
records.reverseExplanation: Et HaOchel supplies the liturgical and institutional structure for these two routes: faith and blessing at the beginning of Zeraim, and the Torah table as an altar in the account of Chullin and Kodashim. Its explicit inclusion of both the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire clarifies what must be directed toward holiness.

records.originHebrew: לְהַעֲלוֹת כָּל מַאֲכָלִים מִצּוֹמֵחַ הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הָאֱמוּנָה לְבַד בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְעַל יְדֵי הַבְּרָכָה מִקֹּדֶם שֶׁמַּאֲמִין שֶׁ"לַה' הָאָרֶץ וּמְלוֹאָהּ"; וּלְכָךְ "אֱמוּנַת" — זֶה סֵדֶר זְרָעִים, וְנִקְבְּעָה מַסֶּכֶת בְּרָכוֹת בִּתְחִלָּתָהּ; וְזֶהוּ הַסֵּדֶר שֶׁל הַעֲלָאַת כָּל מִינֵי הַזְּרָעִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי קִיּוּם הַמִּצְוֹת הַכְּתוּבוֹת בָּהֶם וְהַבְּרָכָה מִקֹּדֶם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָאֱמוּנָה שֶׁהַכֹּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, בֶּאֱמוּנָה הַפְּשׁוּטָה הַקְּבוּעָה בְּלֵב כָּל אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּשַׁבָּת [צ״ז עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁהֵם "מַאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים", וּלְכָךְ הוּתַר אֲפִילּוּ לְעַם הָאָרֶץ. אֲבָל אֲכִילַת בָּשָׂר אָסוּר, רַק לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם; וְלָכֵן נִקְבְּעָה מַסֶּכֶת חֻלִּין בְּסֵדֶר קָדָשִׁים, דְּלֹא הוּתַר אֶלָּא לְמִי שֶׁאוֹכֵל חֻלִּין עַל טָהֳרַת קֹדֶשׁ, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁשֻּׁלְחָנוֹ דּוֹמֶה לַמִּזְבֵּחַ, וְהַבָּשָׂר שֶׁאוֹכֵל כְּקָרְבָּן וּבְשַׂר קֹדֶשׁ. וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: מִשֶּׁחָרַב בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ אֵין לוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶלָּא אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה; וּכְשֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה שֻׁלְחָנוֹ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת שֶׁל הֲלָכָה, אָז הוּא נַעֲשָׂה דֻּגְמַת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ וּמִזְבֵּחַ, וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא אוֹכֵל הוּא דֻּגְמַת כֹּהֲנִים, "כִּי קָא זָכוּ — מִשֻּׁלְחַן גָּבוֹהַּ קָא זָכוּ"; שֶׁהַחֵלֶב וְהַדָּם, רָצָה לוֹמַר עִקַּר הַחִיּוּת שֶׁבַּמַּאֲכָל וְהַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּאָדָם לוֹ, הוּעֲלָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה (שֶׁנִּמְשְׁלוּ לְאֵשׁ שֶׁהוּא אֵשׁ הַמַּעֲרָכָה), שֶׁמַּכִּיר עַל יָדוֹ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן הַחִיּוּת בַּמַּאֲכָל, וְהַנּוֹתֵן הַתַּאֲוָה לָאָדָם וְהַחֵשֶׁק לְזֶה הַמַּאֲכָל לְקַיֵּם נַפְשׁוֹ.
records.originEnglish: Raising all foods that come from plants is accomplished through faith in the blessed God alone, and through the blessing beforehand, by which one believes that “the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord.” Therefore “faith” refers to the order Zeraim, and tractate Berakhot was placed at its beginning. This is the order of raising all kinds of seeds to the blessed God through the fulfillment of their prescribed commandments and the blessing beforehand: the faith that everything belongs to the blessed God. This simple faith is fixed in the heart of every Israelite, as the Sages said in Shabbat that they are “believers, children of believers.” Such food was therefore permitted even to an unlearned person. Eating meat, however, is forbidden except to a Torah scholar. Tractate Chullin was therefore placed in the order Kodashim: it was permitted only to someone who eats ordinary food in the purity of holiness, whose table resembles an altar and whose meat is like an offering and sacred meat. This comes only through words of Torah, as it is written: “Since the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One, blessed be He, has only the four cubits of halakhah.” When one’s table becomes four cubits of halakhah, it resembles the Temple and altar, and what one eats resembles the priests’ eating: “When they receive their share, they receive it from the table of the Most High.” The fat and blood—that is, the principal vitality within the food and the person’s desire for it—have been raised to the blessed God through words of Torah, which are compared to fire, the fire of the altar’s arrangement. Through them one recognizes that the blessed God gives vitality to the food and gives the person desire and longing for this food to sustain his soul.
records.themeTitle: Faith and Torah raise different forms of nourishment
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel distinguishes plant food raised through basic faith and its mitzvot from meat requiring the table to become a place of Torah. The altar image concerns the direction given to both the food’s vitality and the eater’s desire.
records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל הַצּוּרַת אָדָם, עַל יְדֵי אֲכִילָתוֹ שֶׁמַּכְנִיס בְּמֵעָיו וְעוֹבֵד בְּזֶה הַכֹּחַ אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אָז הוּא מְהַפֵּךְ הַדּוֹמֵם וְעוֹשֶׂה מֵהַדּוֹמֵם וּמֵהַצּוֹמֵחַ וּמֵהַחַי בְּחִינַת "מְדַבֵּר" – כִּדְאִיתָא (וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה ב, א): "'כִּי מִדֵּי דַבְּרִי בּוֹ' – דַּי דִּבּוּרִי שֶׁנָּתַתִּי בּוֹ", הַיְינוּ כֹּחַ הַתְּפִלָּה שֶׁנִּיתַּן בָּאָדָם – וְזֶה הוּא עִיקַּר כַּוָּנַת הָאֲכִילָה. וְכַאֲשֶׁר רָאוּ הַמַּלְאָכִים גּוֹדֶל הַכֹּחַ הַזֶּה שֶׁנִּמְצָא בְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (לַהֲפוֹךְ חֹשֶׁךְ לְאוֹר וְגַשְׁמִיּוּת לְרוּחָנִיּוּת), בִּקְּשׁוּ גַּם הֵם לֵיהָנוֹת מִסְּעוּדָה כָּזוֹ שֶׁהוּא מִבְּחִינַת זְעֵיר אַנְפִּין!
records.targetEnglish: The human form, however, through eating—taking the food into his body and serving the blessed God with that strength—transforms the inanimate and makes the inanimate, the plant, and the animal into the level of the speaking being. As it is taught in Vayikra Rabbah: “‘Whenever I speak of him’—the speech that I placed within him is sufficient,” meaning the power of prayer given to the human being. This is the principal intention of eating. When the angels saw the greatness of this power in Abraham our father, of blessed memory—to turn darkness into light and physicality into spirituality—they too sought to benefit from such a meal, which belongs to the aspect of Ze’er Anpin.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov specifies the human activity in which raised nourishment becomes visible: the received strength becomes speech and prayer in the service of God. This illuminates Et HaOchel’s account of the table as an altar and the food’s vitality being raised through Torah. It supplies a concrete destination for that vitality, while Et HaOchel itself provides the distinct account of plant food and meat.

records.originHebrew: כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת לַאֲמִתּוֹ, כָּל הָאֲכִילוֹת שֶׁל אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי הוּא דֻּגְמַת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת, רַק כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ מְבֹרָר לָאָדָם בְּכַוָּנַת לִבּוֹ וּמֹחוֹ הוּא דֻּגְמַת יָשֵׁן, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "בְּשׁוּב ה' וְגוֹמֵר הָיִינוּ כְּחֹלְמִים", וְאִיכָּא אִינָשׁ דְּנָיֵים שִׁבְעִים שְׁנִין, שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי שְׁנוֹתֵינוּ בָּהֶם, כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ מִתְעוֹרֵר מִתַּרְדֵּמַת הַזְּמָן, הֲרֵי הוּא כְּיָשֵׁן; כְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ עוֹשֶׂה אִסּוּרִים מַמָּשׁ רַק בְּהֶתֵּר, עַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה [ס״ה עַמּוּד א׳]: יָכוֹל יְגָרֶה עַצְמוֹ בְּשֵׁנָה (וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּהַהֶתֵּר הוּא מִקְּלִפַּת נֹגַהּ שֶׁהוּא סוֹד הַתַּרְגּוּם, בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא תַּרְדֵּמָה), וְאָמַר: יוֹשֵׁב בָּטֵל כְּיָשֵׁן דָּמֵי. וּכְשֶׁזּוֹכֶה לְהִתְעוֹרֵר פַּעַם אַחַת מִשְּׁנָתוֹ, יוּכַל לְתַקֵּן כָּל הַתַּרְדֵּמוֹת, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תַּרְדֵּמָה שֶׁל נְבוּאָה, כִּדְאִיתָא בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה דְּג׳ תַּרְדֵּמוֹת הֵן וְיֵשׁ שֶׁל נְבוּאָה; כִּי אָז נְבוּאָה בָּאָה עַל יְדֵי אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיִצְחָק (וְכֵן כָּל תַּאֲווֹת דְּהֶתֵּר כְּעִנְיַן "כְּנַגֵּן הַמְנַגֵּן", וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: רַבָּה פָּתַח בְּמִילֵי דִּבְדִיחוּתָא, רַק שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא אַחַר כָּךְ שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה, כְּשֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אַחַר כָּךְ מִצְוָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה הַשִּׂמְחָה וְהַבְּדִיחוּתָא, וְכָל הַהֲנָאוֹת שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִתְעַלֵּית גַּם הֲנָאָה זוֹ לִהְיוֹת שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה); וְכֵן כָּל שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר פַּעַם אַחַת יוּכַל לְהַעֲלוֹת כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו שֶׁל הֶתֵּר וְדִבְרֵי הָרְשׁוּת שֶׁעָשָׂה (וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר מַעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְוֹת בְּלֹא כַּוָּנָה וְחִיּוּת) מִקֹּדֶם, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתָהּ פַּעַם אַחֶרֶת עִם חִיּוּת וְכַוָּנָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם.
records.originEnglish: For in very truth, all the eating of an Israelite resembles offerings. When this is not clarified to the person in the intention of his heart and mind, however, it resembles sleep. As they said: “When the Lord returned ... we were like dreamers”; there is a person who sleeps for seventy years, the years of our lives. When one does not awaken from the slumber of time, he is like a sleeper. This concerns someone who does not commit actual prohibitions but acts within what is permitted. Concerning this they said in Avodah Zarah: “Might he provoke himself to sleep?” [As is known, the permitted belongs to kelipat nogah, the inward meaning of the Aramaic translation, whose numerical value is that of tardemah, slumber.] They said that one who sits idle resembles a sleeper. When one merits awakening once from sleep, one can repair all those slumbers so that they become the slumber of prophecy, as Bereshit Rabbah teaches that there are three kinds of slumber, including that of prophecy. Prophecy then comes through eating and drinking, as is written concerning Isaac. The same applies to all permitted desires, as in “When the musician played,” and in the saying that Rabbah opened with words of humor. This is afterward called the joy of a mitzvah, when one subsequently performs a mitzvah through that joy and humor; with the pleasures of this world, this enjoyment too is raised to become the joy of a mitzvah. Likewise, anyone who awakens once can raise all the permitted acts and matters of choice he performed previously—and certainly mitzvot performed without intention and vitality—by performing that act another time with vitality and intention for the sake of Heaven.
records.themeTitle: One conscious act can awaken earlier permitted acts
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel treats unawakened permitted activity as sleep. Repeating such an act with living intention can clarify and raise the earlier acts; the passage expressly distinguishes this from committing actual prohibitions.
records.targetHebrew: דִּתְפִלָּה אַחַת רְאוּיָה מַעֲלָה עִמָּהּ כַּמָּה תְּפִלּוֹת הַנִּדָּחוֹת וְכֵן מִצְוָה אַחַת שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה מַעֲלָה עִמָּהּ כַּמָּה [דְּנוֹשֵׂא אָדָם כַּמָּה נָשִׁים, וְהוּא דְּאֶפְשָׁר לְמֵיקַם בְּסִפּוּקַיְיהוּ (יְבָמוֹת דַּף ס״ה עַמּוּד ב׳)] מִצְוֹת שֶׁאֵינָם מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה, וְאֵין לָהֶם חַיּוּת בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָם
records.targetEnglish: A single fitting prayer raises with it many rejected prayers. Likewise, one mitzvah performed from wisdom raises with it many mitzvot not performed from wisdom [for a man may marry several women, provided that he can maintain them, as in Yevamot], which have no vitality of their own.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek explains the prayer analogy cited by Et HaOchel through the difference between a living act of wisdom and actions lacking their own vitality. One fitting act can give those earlier acts a place within its life. This supports the retrospective movement in Et HaOchel, whose own quotation explicitly confines this discussion to permitted activity and mitzvot performed without living intention.

records.originEnglish: For in very truth, all the eating of an Israelite resembles offerings. When this is not clarified to the person in the intention of his heart and mind, however, it resembles sleep. As they said: “When the Lord returned ... we were like dreamers”; there is a person who sleeps for seventy years, the years of our lives. When one does not awaken from the slumber of time, he is like a sleeper. This concerns someone who does not commit actual prohibitions but acts within what is permitted. Concerning this they said in Avodah Zarah: “Might he provoke himself to sleep?” [As is known, the permitted belongs to kelipat nogah, the inward meaning of the Aramaic translation, whose numerical value is that of tardemah, slumber.] They said that one who sits idle resembles a sleeper. When one merits awakening once from sleep, one can repair all those slumbers so that they become the slumber of prophecy, as Bereshit Rabbah teaches that there are three kinds of slumber, including that of prophecy. Prophecy then comes through eating and drinking, as is written concerning Isaac. The same applies to all permitted desires, as in “When the musician played,” and in the saying that Rabbah opened with words of humor. This is afterward called the joy of a mitzvah, when one subsequently performs a mitzvah through that joy and humor; with the pleasures of this world, this enjoyment too is raised to become the joy of a mitzvah. Likewise, anyone who awakens once can raise all the permitted acts and matters of choice he performed previously—and certainly mitzvot performed without intention and vitality—by performing that act another time with vitality and intention for the sake of Heaven.
records.themeTitle: One conscious act can awaken earlier permitted acts
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel treats unawakened permitted activity as sleep. Repeating such an act with living intention can clarify and raise the earlier acts; the passage expressly distinguishes this from committing actual prohibitions.
records.targetHebrew: כי על כל עבודות היקרים אמרו ז"ל בגמ' (פסחים ס"ח:) מעיקרא כי עביד אינש לגרמי' הוא דעביד וכדאי' (נזיר כג:) לעולם יעסוק אדם בתורה ובמצות אפילו שלא לשמה שמתוך שלא לשמה בא לשמה ואחר שזוכה האדם לעסוק לשמה אזי נתברר למפרע שאף מה דעביד מתחלה לגרמי' היה ג"כ בזה כבוד שמים וזה הבירור נקרא סוכה והוא כענין מאמרם ז"ל (ברכות ט"ו) הרוצה שיקבל עליו עול מלכות שמים שלימה יפנה ויטול ידיו ויניח תפילין ויקרא ק"ש ויתפלל היינו שיכול להתפלל אף על צרכי גופו כי ע"י הקבלת עומ"ש נתבררו אצלו גם צרכי גופו שהם כבוד שמים
records.targetEnglish: Concerning all precious forms of service, the Sages said in Pesachim: “At first, when a person acts, he acts for himself.” As it is taught in Nazir: “A person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for from acting not for their own sake he comes to act for their own sake.” After a person merits engaging for its own sake, it becomes clarified retrospectively that even what he first did for himself also contained the glory of Heaven. This clarification is called sukkah. It is like the Sages’ saying in Berakhot: “One who wishes to accept the complete yoke of the kingdom of Heaven should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, recite Shema, and pray.” This means that he can pray even for his bodily needs, for through accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, his bodily needs too become clarified as the glory of Heaven.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim describes the retrospective clarification that follows a later act done for its own sake. The earlier self-directed work is then recognized within the movement toward service, and bodily needs can also be brought into that acceptance of Heaven’s rule. This illuminates Et HaOchel’s awakening of prior permitted actions without substituting a claim that a later intention automatically authorizes forbidden acts.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Later service for its own sake clarifies earlier beginnings
records.reverseThemeSummary: Within its account of sukkah as a conscious bridge to a deeper protection, Sod Yesharim explains how service for its own sake can clarify earlier work done for oneself and bring bodily needs into accepted Divine service.
records.reverseExplanation: Et HaOchel makes this retrospective clarification concrete through repeated acts of eating and other permitted activities. Its sleep-and-awakening comparison distinguishes an unawakened beginning from the later act that gives it conscious vitality, while explicitly retaining the boundary against actual prohibitions.

records.originEnglish: [Solomon] asked that his food also be “prey.” This is through “my allotted bread”: within a boundary, neither with ravenous eating and an abundance of desire, called “wealth,” nor with excessive hunger and deprivation. As they said, one who sits fasting is called a sinner; the meaning is that he withholds the raising of the holiness in food to its place through eating. Only “the belly of the wicked shall lack”: it is fitting to restrict oneself and fast in order to eliminate ravenousness. But a righteous person who is neither ravenous nor immersed in desire “eats to satisfy his soul”—that is, his allotted bread. Through this he can reach the level of “provide me with prey,” seizing and capturing the good within the evil so that it is included in the good. This is the meaning of “He gave prey to those who fear Him.” Those who fear Him set especially strong boundaries against desires, and through this can come to withhold even their allotted bread. The Holy One, blessed be He, gives them “prey” as a gift: to eat at least their allotted bread, in order to capture those holy sparks within the food.
records.themeTitle: An allotted portion preserves the work that eating can accomplish
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel distinguishes measured nourishment from both ravenous consumption and excessive deprivation. Even someone strongly committed to restraint may need to receive enough food to accomplish the holy purpose of eating.
records.targetHebrew: רַק שֶׁהוּא דַּי לוֹ בְּקַב, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "מַשְׂבִּיעַ לְכָל חַי רָצוֹן" כְּפִי רְצוֹנוֹ, וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּקֵּשׁ "הַטְרִיפֵנִי לֶחֶם חֻקִּי" כְּפִי צֹרֶךְ הַלֶּחֶם שֶׁלּוֹ בִּסְעֻדַּת שְׁלֹמֹה בִּשְׁעָתָהּ, וְזֶה נֶחְשָׁב אֶצְלוֹ לְלֶחֶם חֻקִּי כְּפִי צֹרֶךְ פַּרְנָסָתוֹ, וְלֹא מוֹתָרוֹת, דְּבִקֵּשׁ עַל זֶה: "רֵישׁ וָעֹשֶׁר אַל תִּתֶּן לִי", לֹא שֶׁיֶּחְסַר לוֹ מִכְּדֵי צָרְכּוֹ וְלֹא מוֹתָרוֹת; וְאֵצֶל רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא נֶחְשָׁב קַב חֲרוּבִין לֶחֶם חֻקִּי, וְיוֹתֵר מִזֶּה הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ מוֹתָרוֹת וְעֹשֶׁר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְבַקֵּשׁ עַל זֶה שֶׁ"אַל תִּתֶּן לִי", וְרֵישׁוּתוֹ הָיָה פָּחוֹת גַּם מִקַּב חֲרוּבִין, וְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ נִזּוֹן בִּשְׁבִילוֹ כָּל אֶחָד בְּלֶחֶם חֻקּוֹ, מִי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ כִּסְעֻדַּת שְׁלֹמֹה וְסוּס לִרְכֹּב וְעֶבֶד לָרוּץ לְפָנָיו, כָּל הִצְטָרְכוּתוֹ הוּא בִּכְלַל מְזוֹנֵי הַנִּמְשָׁךְ לְכָל אֶחָד בִּשְׁבִילוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: It is only that a kav is enough for him, for the blessed God “satisfies the desire of every living thing” according to that creature’s desire. King Solomon, peace be upon him, asked, “Provide me with my allotted bread,” according to the bread he needed at a meal of Solomon in his time. For him this counted as his allotted bread, according to his need for sustenance, and was not surplus. It was about this that he asked, “Give me neither poverty nor wealth”: neither a lack of what he needed nor surplus. For Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, a kav of carobs counted as his allotted bread; more than this would have been surplus and wealth, concerning which he should ask, “Do not give me.” His poverty was having less even than a kav of carobs. The whole world is sustained on his account, each person with his own allotted bread. Whoever needs a meal like Solomon’s, a horse to ride, and a servant to run before him—all his needs are included in the sustenance drawn to each person on his account.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains why “allotted bread” is a personal measure rather than a single small quantity for everyone. Solomon’s abundant meal and Rabbi Chanina’s kav can each represent need rather than surplus. This specifies the balance in Et HaOchel: the aim is to receive what serves the person’s task, without confusing deprivation with holiness or appetite with need.

records.reverseThemeTitle: A person’s real need can become the opening for others’ provision
records.reverseThemeSummary: Divrei Soferim explains how a righteous person’s own need and prayer can open provision for others. Its comparison of Solomon and Rabbi Chanina makes clear that each recipient has a different measure of what counts as necessary sustenance.
records.reverseExplanation: Et HaOchel explains the work accomplished by receiving one’s allotted nourishment. It identifies both ravenous excess and excessive deprivation as obstacles to raising the food’s vitality, giving practical content to Divrei Soferim’s distinction between personal need and surplus.

records.originEnglish: Likewise, in the Zohar it is everywhere called warfare with swords and bows, and the time of eating is called “the time of battle.” For raising the sparks occurs through the good inclination’s victory over the evil inclination: the food that gives the body life sustains only its good power and good inclination, and not its evil power. The good power wins the battle to seize the holy spark and the food’s vitality for its own share.
records.themeTitle: The meal’s battle concerns which power receives its vitality
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel explains “seizing” through the destination of the food’s life: the good inclination must receive the strength that could instead sustain the evil inclination. The surrounding paragraph explicitly joins this battle to measured eating.
records.targetHebrew: ורק הענין בזה, מחמת שהשי"ת הציב בזה העולם אילנא דספיקא והיינו שהציב השי"ת הסתרות אור בזה העולם, על כן הציב השי"ת דברי רשות ונתן לאדם בחירה, שיהיה בכח בחירתו לברר הדברים האלה על ידי עבודתו, וכמו שכתיב (משלי כ״ג:א׳) כי תשב ללחום את מושל בין תבין את אשר לפניך. וכן איתא בזוה"ק (עקב ער"ב.) שעת סעודה שעת קרבא, והיינו שאם האדם ילך בכח בחירתו ויברר עצמו באלו הדברים ויחזירם להשי"ת פנים בפנים, אז הוא מנצח את המאכל, ולהיפך להיפך. וזה מורה ענין רשות, שיש לאדם בחירה חפשית בזה ויכול לברר עצמו בכח בחירתו. ובאמת כל הענין שהציב השי"ת זה הוא מחמת שהשי"ת חפץ להיטיב לבריותיו, ורצה שהאדם יהיה לו חלק בהטובה, על כן הציב השי"ת את זה. ואם האדם באמת יברר עצמו יחזירם להשי"ת פנים בפנים, אז יהיה נקרא השכר יגיע כפיך כי תאכל וגו'.
records.targetEnglish: The matter is that the blessed God placed the “tree of doubt” in this world—that is, He placed concealments of light in this world. He therefore established matters of permission and gave a person choice, so that, through the power of his choice, he could clarify these things by his service. As it is written, “When you sit to dine with a ruler, understand well what is before you.” Likewise, it is taught in the holy Zohar: “The time of a meal is the time of battle.” If a person proceeds with the power of his choice, clarifies himself in these things, and returns them to the blessed God face to face, he then overcomes the food; and conversely, the reverse. This is what permission indicates: a person has free choice in it and can clarify himself through that choice. In truth, God established this entire matter because He desires to benefit His creatures and wanted the person to have a share in the good. If the person truly clarifies himself and returns these things to the blessed God face to face, the reward will then be called, “When you eat the labor of your hands,” and so forth.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef uses the same image of a meal as battle and explains why this struggle exists within permitted activity. The concealment allows the eater’s choice and service to contribute to the good received. This adds the purpose of the struggle to Et HaOchel’s account of its outcome: the food’s power must be returned toward God, rather than overcoming the eater. The rest of Tiferet Yosef preserves abstention as the appropriate response when a person cannot yet accomplish that return.

records.originHebrew: מִצְוַת אֲכִילַת מַצָּה נוֹתֶנֶת קְדוּשָׁה בָּאֲכִילוֹת, כִּי כָּל מִצְוָה, בִּפְרָט אוֹתָהּ שֶׁמְּבָרְכִין עָלֶיהָ "אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ", מוֹסֶפֶת קְדוּשָׁה בָּאָדָם, וּבְיִחוּד בְּאוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר וְכֹחַ שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ נַעֲשֵׂית, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה [פָּרָשָׁה כ״א:ה׳]: "עָשִׂיתָ חֲבִילוֹת עֲבֵרוֹת — עֲשֵׂה נֶגְדָּן חֲבִילוֹת מִצְוֹת... יָדַיִם וְכוּלֵי";
records.originEnglish: The mitzvah of eating matzah gives holiness to acts of eating. Every mitzvah—especially one over which we bless, “Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us”—adds holiness to a person, particularly to the limb and faculty through which it is performed. As our Sages said in Vayikra Rabbah: “If you have made bundles of transgressions, make corresponding bundles of mitzvot ... hands,” and so forth.
records.themeTitle: A particular mitzvah can form the way a faculty is used afterward
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel explains the Seder foods as more than a single holy meal. A mitzvah sanctifies the faculty that performs it, and the matzah meal thereby bears on the bread eaten throughout the year.
records.targetRef: Sod Yesharim, Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot 20:3
records.targetHebrew: והנה בזמן החורף אז מחזק השי"ת השרשים והיסודות גבי האדם. לזה בסוף החורף כאשר מתחלף מחורף לקיץ צריך האדם לאכול מצה שנקרא מיכלא דמהימנותא מיכלא דאסוותא. היינו שמרגיל את האדם לבלתי יקבל רק מה שמבורר מאד וממילא יהיה אחר כך בקיץ שהוא זמן הצמיחה כל הענפים שיצמחו נמי מבוררים היטב:
records.targetEnglish: During winter, the blessed God strengthens the roots and foundations within a person. Therefore, at the end of winter, when winter changes to summer, the person must eat matzah, which is called “the food of faith” and “the food of healing.” It trains a person to receive only what is very clearly clarified. Consequently, afterward in summer, the season of growth, all the branches that grow will also be thoroughly clarified.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains the passage from a foundational act to later growth. Matzah trains reception at the root, so that what subsequently develops from it can be clarified as well. This gives a concrete account of how the single seasonal mitzvah in Et HaOchel can affect eating beyond the Seder itself, without asserting that every later meal is automatically sanctified regardless of conduct.

records.originHebrew: וְהִנֵּה גְּאֻלַּת מִצְרַיִם הוּא עַל יְדֵי לְאַכְפַּיָּא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר עַל "וַיִּקַּח מֹשֶׁה אֶת עַצְמוֹת יוֹסֵף עִמּוֹ" [שְׁמוֹת י״ג:י״ט], לָכֵן נִצְטַוּוּ עַל בִּעוּר חָמֵץ, וְהָיוּ גַּם כֵּן חֵרוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע רַק בְּדֶרֶךְ הַסִּלּוּק לְגַמְרֵי, מִדַּת צַדִּיק גָּמוּר; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא זְבִיחַת הַיֵּצֶר בְּעִנְיַן לְאִתְהַפְּכָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם דְּיִהְיֶה גַּם אָז יֵצֶר הָרָע לְחֶדְוָתָא דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, רַק דְּנִקְרָא לָבָן דְּאִתְלַבַּן וְכוּלֵי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר דְּזֶה סוֹד סְעוּדַת לִוְיָתָן וְשׁוֹר הַבָּר, שֶׁהֵם יִצְרָא דַּעֲרָיוֹת וּדְעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מֵהֶם מַאֲכָל טוֹב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "טוֹב מְאֹד" — זֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע [בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה ט׳:ז׳], עַל יְדֵי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה זֶה בְּמִצְרַיִם.
records.originEnglish: The redemption from Egypt came through subduing, as I have written elsewhere concerning “Moses took Joseph’s bones with him.” They were therefore commanded to remove chametz, and they were also free of the evil inclination, but only by its complete removal—the quality of the wholly righteous person. By contrast, in the future, the slaughter of the inclination will be through transformation. As it is written in the Midrash HaNe’elam, there will even then be an evil inclination for the joy of Torah, but it will be called “white,” for it has been whitened, and so forth. As I have written elsewhere, this is the inward meaning of the feast of Leviathan and the wild ox: they are the inclinations toward sexual transgression and idolatry, from which good food will be made. As they said, “‘Very good’—this is the evil inclination.” This is through King David, peace be upon him, who established the yoke of repentance; this was not present in Egypt.
records.themeTitle: The power first restrained must ultimately be turned toward good
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel distinguishes removing the force of desire from transforming it into the joy of Torah. The section later insists that suppression alone cannot accomplish the complete victory within human life.
records.targetHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ, כִּי מִי שֶׁהוֹלֵךְ בַּמִּלְחָמָה, הוֹלֵךְ נֶגֶד חֲבֵירוֹ: וְאִם חֲבֵירוֹ מַבְעִיר אֵשׁ נֶגְדּוֹ, הוּא נוֹתֵן מַיִם וּמְכַבֶּה; אֲבָל מִי שֶׁכְּבָר נִצַּח וְהוּא שֶׁלּוֹ, כָּל הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁעָשָׂה הָאוֹיֵב נֶגְדּוֹ כְּדֵי לִלְחוֹם עִמּוֹ הוּא מְתַקְּנָם לְצָרְכּוֹ, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ מִשְׁתַּמְּשִׁים אוֹתוֹ תַּשְׁמִישׁ לְצָרְכּוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: When someone goes to war, he goes against his opponent: if his opponent kindles fire against him, he puts water on it and extinguishes it. But one who has already won, so that it is his, repairs for his own use everything the enemy employed against him in the battle, so that it serves the same function for his own purposes.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains the sequence that Et HaOchel distinguishes through Egypt and the future. During battle, one counters the hostile power; after actual victory, the power itself can be put to holy use. This preserves the condition on transformation: the later use of desire is not a substitute for restraint while it still controls the person. Et HaOchel adds why the process must ultimately reach beyond suppression.

records.reverseThemeTitle: The enemy’s power can be used only after it has been overcome
records.reverseThemeSummary: Kometz HaMinchah distinguishes resistance during a struggle from raising a conquered power to its source. Its examples of Joseph, David, and the rainbow explain different forms of restraint and attained holiness.
records.reverseExplanation: Et HaOchel develops the difference into a larger account of redemption: the removal of chametz expresses subduing, while the future feast expresses the transformation of the very inclinations into good. Its insistence that suppression alone cannot complete human repair clarifies the purpose of the later use of power described in Kometz HaMinchah.

records.originHebrew: כִּי בְּלֹא מָזוֹן אִי אֶפְשָׁר, דְּכָךְ יִסֵּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִהְיוֹת כָּל נִבְרָא בַּעַל גְּבוּל צָרִיךְ לְמָזוֹן הַמְקַיֵּם כֹּחַ חִיּוּתוֹ, רַק שֶׁאָז יִהְיֶה מֻפְשָׁט מִלְּבוּשׁ, וְיִהְיֶה הַמָּזוֹן זִיו הַשְּׁכִינָה; וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בִּלְבוּשׁ, אֲבָל הַבְּרָכָה הוּא הַהַכָּרָה מַה שֶּׁבְּתוֹךְ הַלְּבוּשׁ וּבִפְנִימִיּוּתוֹ.
records.originEnglish: For it is impossible to be without nourishment: the blessed God founded the world so that every bounded creature needs nourishment that sustains its power of life. Only then [in the World to Come] it will be stripped of clothing, and the nourishment will be the radiance of the Divine Presence. In this world it is clothed; but the blessing is the recognition of what lies within the clothing, in its inwardness.
records.themeTitle: Blessing recognizes the life within the food’s clothing
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel explains Rebbi’s table through the difference between treating taste and vitality as the food’s independent property and recognizing the Divine life clothed within them. Blessing makes the inward giver present to the eater.
records.targetHebrew: בתחלה מברכין המוציא לחם מן הארץ וכמאמרם ז"ל בגמרא (ברכות ל"ח) המוציא דאפיק משמע. וגם ברכה הוא לישנא דאמשכותא שממשיך אליו את המוצא פי ה' המתלבש בהמאכל כדכתיב כי לא על הלחם לבדו יחיה האדם כי על כל מוצא פי ה' היינו שהרצון יתברך מבריאת עולם שמהוה ומחיה כל הדברים שבעולם זה הרצון נתלבש בהלחם ומחיה את האדם וע"י הברכה בוקע אדם את הלבושים ומוצא ומפיק אליו את הרצון יתברך המחיה את האדם וקודם האכילה בשעת הברכה אז האדם משפיע להמאכל כי ע"י הברכה נתעלה המאכל. אבל בשעת האכילה אז נקרא המאכל משפיע כי האדם ניזון מהמאכל ולאחר האכילה האדם הוא גבר על המאכל כי אז הוא הבחירה ביד אדם כפי אשר יעבוד לה' בכח האכילה ההיא כך יהיה עליה לזה המאכל
records.targetEnglish: At the beginning we bless, “Who brings bread forth from the earth,” as the Sages said in Berakhot: “Ha-motzi means ‘who brought forth.’” Blessing is also an expression of drawing forth: one draws to oneself the utterance of God’s mouth clothed within the food. As it is written, “For a person does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds from God’s mouth.” The blessed will that, from the creation of the world, brings into being and gives life to everything in the world is clothed within the bread and gives life to the person. Through the blessing, the person breaks through the garments and finds and draws forth to himself the blessed will that gives him life. Before eating, at the time of the blessing, the person gives to the food, for through the blessing the food is raised. But at the time of eating, the food is called the giver, because the person is nourished by it. After eating, the person prevails over the food, because the choice is then in his hands: according to the way he serves God with the strength of that eating, so will be the ascent of that food.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains recognition through a sequence of giving and receiving. The blessing draws out the Divine will within the food; the food then sustains the person; afterward, the person’s chosen service determines its ascent. This supplies an active account of the “recognition within the clothing” in Et HaOchel and preserves the responsibility that follows the recognition.

records.originEnglish: Therefore Rebbi was the one who arranged the Mishnah, which is the foundation of the Oral Torah, as Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was for the Written Torah. Moses was literally among those who ate manna: it was visibly revealed that the bread came from Heaven. Accordingly, the Written Torah is explicit that the bread truly comes from God, like the Written Torah that is already written and set before us. This continued as long as prophecy existed, for prophecy too is an explicit word from God; afterward the jar of manna was hidden away. The inquiry into this under concealment—to understand it through one’s own knowledge and understanding—is the Oral Torah, established as a written text set before us through Rebbi. He clarified this even under concealment: bread from the earth is only from God. This is the whole essence of the Oral Torah: Israel’s wisdom also comes from the blessed God. This is a great power, for it makes the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil into the Tree of Life. Moses our teacher’s power was from the Tree of Life itself; this one grasped the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil and made it the Tree of Life. Understand this. Therefore they said that whoever studies halakhot—meaning the Mishnah—is assured that he is a child of the World to Come, that is, the eternal life of the Tree of Life.
records.themeTitle: Oral Torah recognizes Divine wisdom within earthly understanding
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel compares Moses and Rebbi through revealed manna and the inward recognition of ordinary bread. The Oral Torah’s human reasoning can recognize its own Divine source even when that source is concealed.

records.targetEnglish: Just as the difference between the Written Torah and the Oral Torah is that the former is the blessed God’s wisdom and the latter is human wisdom—except that people recognize that it too comes from the blessed God, and it thereby also becomes a complete Torah and the blessed God’s wisdom—so is the difference between the manna eaten by the wilderness generation, who received the Written Torah, when it was explicitly visible as bread from Heaven, and the manna of later generations, which is bread from the earth. Through recognizing that it comes from the blessed God, it too becomes “bread from Heaven.” This happens through the spread of the full stature of the lower wisdom, the Oral Torah, within the hearts of Israel. It began immediately upon entry into the land, when the manna ceased.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz makes the analogy in Et HaOchel explicit and locates its beginning at entry into the land. The cessation of visible manna requires recognition of the giver within earthly provision, just as Oral Torah recognizes the Divine source within human understanding. This explains why Rebbi’s achievement is associated with concealment and active understanding, rather than simply with abstention from enjoyable food.

records.originEnglish: Matzah is called “the food of healing”; certainly it heals the wound of the world, as our Sages expounded the verse “He will heal the wound of His striking.” This is the unspecified healing of a wound in Scripture. (This also explains “For I am the Lord who heals you.” Our Sages asked: if there is no blow, why is healing needed? The meaning is that God also heals the wound of the world, and consequently “all the illness,” and so forth. The Exodus from Egypt prepares for the giving of the Torah, which heals the world’s wound; presumably, then, the plagues of Egypt were because they opposed this.) This concerns the power of eating. Nevertheless, there is still death because of the serpent’s instigation. This means what our Sages said: the serpent came and introduced impurity. That impurity is in sexual desire, concerning which they said that even the most pious person cannot be entirely without a trace of evil—as with [Jesse], who was one of the four who died through the serpent’s instigation. Only Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai, had their impurity cease; then they were truly free of the evil inclination and the angel of death, had it not been for the later sin.
records.themeTitle: Healing the earlier appetite prepares for a deeper repair
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel does not identify the sanctification of eating with the immediate completion of every repair. Matzah addresses the earlier wound and prepares for Torah’s work against a further impurity, while the discussion retains the interruption caused by later sin.

records.targetHebrew: מצה שנקרא בזהר מיכלא דאסיותא ולא נזכר למה הוא רפואה מסתמא הוא רפואה למחץ מכתו של עולם וכמ"ד חטה היה. וכשאוכלים זה המאכל מחטה לקיים מצות ד' נתקן אותה אכילה דאיסור. ועל כן יהיה תחה"מ בפסח כשאז"ל כי על ידי אכילת מצה בכל פסח נתקן מעט עד שיתוקן לגמרי ואז יבולע המות לנצח אף בבע"ח כמ"ש זאב וטלה ירעו כאחד וגו'. ואז"ל (בב"ר פצ"ה) דהכל מתרפאין כי גם הם על ידי אדם הראשון שהאכיל לכולם נגזר עליהם אף שאין להם דעת. דלא עדיפי מאדם שכולם נבראו בשבילו וכשהוא יתוקן גם הם יתוקנו חוץ מאותו רשע שהוריד הבריות לעפר שהוא התחלת הקלקול ולא יועיל מה שהאדם יתוקן לו.
records.targetEnglish: Matzah is called in the Zohar “the food of healing,” without specifying what it heals. Presumably it heals the wound of the world, according to the view that the Tree [of Knowledge] was wheat. When this food made from wheat is eaten to fulfill God’s command, that forbidden eating is repaired. The resurrection of the dead will therefore take place on Pesach, as our Sages said, for through eating matzah each Pesach a little is repaired, until it is completely repaired. Then death will be swallowed up forever, even among animals, as it is written, “The wolf and the lamb will graze together,” and so forth. Our Sages said in Bereshit Rabbah that all are healed, for they too were condemned through Adam, who fed all of them, even though they have no understanding. They cannot fare better than Adam, since all were created for him; when he is repaired, they too will be repaired—except for that wicked one who brought creatures down to the dust, for he was the beginning of the corruption, and the repair of the human being will not help him.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik explicitly describes repair through successive Pesachs: each eating of matzah repairs a little, until the wound is fully healed. This guards the sequence in Et HaOchel against being read as an immediate claim that a single meal has already removed every consequence of the first sin. The relation is the author’s theological account of gradual repair, with the serpent’s distinct role and the eventual completion preserved.

records.originEnglish: Matzah is called “the food of healing”; certainly it heals the wound of the world, as our Sages expounded the verse “He will heal the wound of His striking.” This is the unspecified healing of a wound in Scripture. (This also explains “For I am the Lord who heals you.” Our Sages asked: if there is no blow, why is healing needed? The meaning is that God also heals the wound of the world, and consequently “all the illness,” and so forth. The Exodus from Egypt prepares for the giving of the Torah, which heals the world’s wound; presumably, then, the plagues of Egypt were because they opposed this.) This concerns the power of eating. Nevertheless, there is still death because of the serpent’s instigation. This means what our Sages said: the serpent came and introduced impurity. That impurity is in sexual desire, concerning which they said that even the most pious person cannot be entirely without a trace of evil—as with [Jesse], who was one of the four who died through the serpent’s instigation. Only Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai, had their impurity cease; then they were truly free of the evil inclination and the angel of death, had it not been for the later sin.
records.themeTitle: Healing the earlier appetite prepares for a deeper repair
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel does not identify the sanctification of eating with the immediate completion of every repair. Matzah addresses the earlier wound and prepares for Torah’s work against a further impurity, while the discussion retains the interruption caused by later sin.

records.targetHebrew: אמנם מצה נקרא לחם מן הארץ שיש בזה עדיין פסולת. ואכילת המן נקרא לחם מן השמים כי לא הי' בזה הלחם שום פסולת שלא הצריכו לנקבים ונהמא דחברייא אכלין הנקרא חכמה תחי' בעלי' הוא מבשמת כל הפסולות ומאירה כל המקומות הרחוקים שאינו נמצא מקום פנוי מאורו ית' וזהו בקדמיתא וכו' עאלו בנהמא דאקרי מצה. והשתא זכו ועאלו למיכל נהמא אחרא עלאה יתיר וכו' היינו ע"י שמסרו כל כח פעולתם להשי"ת כי חמץ מורה על פעולת אדם ומצה על שלולות פעולת אדם כמבואר ולכך זכו ללחם מן השמים שהוא מבורר לגמרי מפסולת כי שמים מורה על בהירות עצום ששם מבורר שהשי"ת הוא הבורא ומנהיג ולכן אין באכילה הזאת שום פסולת כלל
records.targetEnglish: Matzah is called bread from the earth, which still contains waste. Eating manna is called bread from Heaven, because that bread contained no waste at all: they did not need to relieve themselves. The bread eaten by the companions, called “Wisdom gives life to its possessors,” sweetens all the waste and illuminates all the distant places, so that no place is found empty of His blessed light. This is “At first ... they entered into the bread called matzah; now they merited and entered into eating another, higher bread,” and so forth. Through handing all the power of their action over to the blessed God—for chametz indicates human action, and matzah the relinquishment of human action, as explained—they merited bread from Heaven, entirely clarified of waste. Heaven indicates an immense clarity, where it is clear that the blessed God is the Creator and Ruler; therefore this eating contains no waste at all.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes three stages, rather than treating every holy food as the same attainment: matzah, manna without waste, and wisdom that sweetens what had been waste. This illuminates Et HaOchel’s insistence that the repair begun in eating prepares for a further work of Torah. The explanations remain distinct: Et HaOchel describes successive repairs of appetite, while Sod Yesharim describes relinquishment, clarity, and eventual transformation.

records.originHebrew: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְכָל מַאֲכָל כֹּחַ מְיֻחָד לְהַחֲיוֹת אֶת הַגּוּף, כָּךְ מִסְּתָמָא יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ חִיּוּת פְּנִימִי הַמְחַיֶּה אֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ; וּמִסְּתָמָא שִׁבְעַת הַמִּינִים שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּבְּחָה בָּהֶם אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם כְּנֶגֶד שֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת הַיְדוּעוֹת שֶׁבַּנֶּפֶשׁ, וּתְמָרִים הֵם הָאַחֲרוֹנָה שֶׁבָּהֶם. וְשָׁמַעְתִּי שֶׁלָּכֵן דָּרְשׁוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּסוֹף תַּעֲנִית (כ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳): "אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה" [יִרְמְיָהוּ כ״ט:י״א] — אֵלּוּ תְּמָרִים וּפִשְׁתָּן; פִּשְׁתָּן מִשּׁוּם "תִּקְוַת חוּט" [יְהוֹשֻׁעַ ב׳:י״ח], וְאַחֲרִית מִשּׁוּם שֶׁהוּא הָאַחֲרוֹן מִשִּׁבְעַת הַמִּינִים, וְנִרְאֶה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ לְבַקֵּשׁ הַקֵּץ. וּבִפְסָחִים [פ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁגָּלוּ לְבָבֶל כְּדֵי שֶׁיֹּאכְלוּ תְּמָרִים וְיַעַסְקוּ בַּתּוֹרָה, הַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁנִּקְבְּעָה בְּבָבֶל; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי שֶׁדְּבַשׁ מַרְגִּיל אֶת הַלָּשׁוֹן לַתּוֹרָה, וּלְכָךְ נִקְרָא בַּתּוֹרָה "דְּבַשׁ" וְלֹא תְּמָרִים; וּמַלְכוּת, שֶׁהִיא הַפֶּה, נִקְרֵאת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּתִקּוּנֵי זֹהַר [תִּקּוּן י״ז עַמּוּד א׳].
records.originEnglish: Just as every food has a particular power to give life to the body, so presumably it has an inward power of life that gives life to the soul. Presumably the seven species for which the Land of Israel is praised correspond to the seven known qualities of the soul, and dates are the last of them. I heard that this is why our Sages expounded at the end of Taanit, “‘A latter end and hope’—these are dates and flax.” Flax is because of “the cord of thread,” and “a latter end” is because it is the last of the seven species; it appears that it has the power to seek the end [of exile]. In Pesachim they say that Israel was exiled to Babylon in order to eat dates and engage in Torah—that is, the Oral Torah established in Babylon. As it is written in the Jerusalem Talmud, honey accustoms the tongue to Torah; therefore it is called “honey” in the Torah, rather than dates. Malkhut, which is the mouth, is called the Oral Torah, as it is written in Tikkunei Zohar.
records.themeTitle: Dates join the Oral Torah of exile to its hope for an end
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel connects the last of the seven species with the final quality, speech and Oral Torah. The nourishment associated with Babylon therefore bears a hope that reaches beyond the present exile.
records.targetHebrew: וזה שנדרש ע"ז (תענית כ"ט:) אלו דקלים וכלי פשתן שהוא מרמז לתושבע"פ שבבבל היו דקלים וכמו שא' (פסחים פ"ח רע"א) לא הגלה הקב"ה את ישראל לבבל וכו' עולא אמר כדי שיאכלו תמרים ויעסקו בתורה. וכלי פשתן הוא מה שא' (קידושין ע"ב.) ת"ח שבבבל דומים למלאכי השרת שהיו מצוינים במלבושיהם (שבת קמ"ה:) והיינו בכלי פשתן לבנים כמלאכי השרת. ורבינו הק' זצ"ל אמר דאחרית פי' בחי' תושבע"פ שהוא מדה אחרונה מלכות פה תושבע"פ קרינן לה. ומרמז ע"ז דקלים שהוא מין האחרון מן הז' מינים דבש תמרים שבכל מקום מספר ז' מרמז כנגד ז' המדות וזהו אחרית. ותקוה היינו בעתיד ששמעתי מרבינו הקדוש זצ"ל שאמר בשם הרבי ר' בינם זצלה"ה שאמר שאף שהדורות המוחות מתמעטין בכל פעם אבל נקודת החיים שבלב מתרחב תמיד ונעשה מזוכך בכל פעם בגלות יותר. ואמר רבינו הק' שהי' לו זה לדבר חדש כששמעו בפשיסחא ואח"כ מצא הדבר מפורש בכמה דוכתי ולא פי' לן אי' מקומן וכבר אמרנו שורש לזה (ונת' במ"א) וזה הוא התקוה טובה בגלות.
records.targetEnglish: This is why they expounded it in Taanit as “palm trees and linen garments,” alluding to the Oral Torah. There were palms in Babylon, as they said in Pesachim: “The Holy One, blessed be He, exiled Israel to Babylon ... Ulla said: so that they would eat dates and engage in Torah.” The linen garments correspond to their statement in Kiddushin that the Torah scholars of Babylon resemble ministering angels, since they were distinguished in their clothing, as in Shabbat—that is, in white linen garments like ministering angels. Our holy teacher, of blessed memory, said that “a latter end” means the Oral Torah, which is the last quality: “Malkhut is the mouth; we call it the Oral Torah.” The palm trees allude to this, for date honey is the last of the seven species, and wherever the number seven appears it alludes to the seven qualities; this is “a latter end.” “Hope” concerns the future. I heard from our holy teacher, of blessed memory, in the name of Rabbi Bunim, of blessed memory, that although the minds of the generations continually diminish, the point of life in the heart constantly expands and becomes more refined in exile. Our holy teacher said that this was a new idea for him when he heard it in Pshischa; afterward he found it explicit in several places, though he did not tell us where. We have already stated a basis for this, as explained elsewhere. This is the good hope within exile.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik unpacks both parts of the expression that Et HaOchel associates with dates. “A latter end” names the Oral Torah’s place in the ordering of the qualities, while “hope” points to the continuing refinement of the heart in exile. This adds a specific account of what can grow under concealment, so that the date’s association with Babylon expresses more than a repeated food symbol.

records.originEnglish: In Eruvin they say: there are two palm trees in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, and the entrance to Gehinnom is there. This is “The righteous person will flourish like a palm”—precisely from the entrance to Gehinnom and from the depths. As it is written in Rosh Hashanah: the sinners of Israel cry out and ascend. This is the power of the date, and this is the good latter end: all this is for a good latter end, so that no one banished from Him will remain banished.
records.themeTitle: The palm’s flourishing expresses repair even from the depths
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel reads the palm’s growth near the entrance to Gehinnom as a sign of an eventual good outcome. The image concerns ascent and repair from the depths, not merely the sweetness of a fruit.
records.targetHebrew: כפת תמרים. זה הוא כדאיתא בכתבי האר"י הק' ז"ל צדיק כתמר יפרח סופי תיבות קר"ח שזאת המדה רומז שאין שום דבר בישראל שיהיה נחלט ח"ו בלי תיקון שלא יהיה חוזר להשורש אף שלפעמים צריך לשהות זמן רב עד התיקון עכ"ז לא ידח ממנו שום נדח:
records.targetEnglish: “Branches of date palms.” This corresponds to what is taught in the writings of the holy Ari, of blessed memory: the final letters of “The righteous person will flourish like a palm” spell Korach. This quality indicates that nothing within Israel will, God forbid, be permanently left without repair, without returning to its root. Even though it is sometimes necessary to remain for a long time until the repair, nevertheless “no one banished from Him will remain banished.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim interprets the same palm verse through Korach and the promise of return to the root. Its explicit qualification—that repair may take a long time—makes the good ending in Et HaOchel more precise. The connection concerns eventual repair from a fallen condition; it does not erase the process or its duration.

records.targetEnglish: In the Gemara, Pesachim: “Bread of poverty—over which many words are answered.” This means that it must take the form of question and answer: the son asks “What is different?” and his father answers him. As it says there: his son asks him, and so forth; his wife asks him; otherwise he asks himself. Likewise, in Rabban Gamliel’s statement: “This matzah that we eat—on account of what?” and so forth; “Maror—on account of what?” and so forth. We do not simply say, “The matzah that we eat is because they did not have enough time,” and so forth, but proceed by question and answer; this is also the Rosh’s reading. On this night a person must feel something new within himself, for he must see himself as though he left Egypt. At that time the person felt a powerful sense within himself of having emerged from the inclination. So every person must feel, on every Pesach night, as though he left Egypt. Eating matzah, maror, and the like must not be a matter of habit for him. Likewise, they said that the entire institution of the first dipping was so that it would be noticeable to the children. This means that the person should awaken to “What makes this night different from all other nights?”—that there is a change here, and he should emerge from habit.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik explains what makes the question an actual opening rather than a ceremonial formula. The changes at the Seder interrupt habit so that the person feels a newly experienced departure from the inclination. This clarifies the lived questioning in Et HaOchel: the answer can expand the heart because a real need to understand has first been awakened.

records.targetEnglish: That is, because completeness is clarified precisely through its opposite, Israel had to be in exile under the enslavement of Egypt, a place more degraded and lowly than the rest of the world, called “the nakedness of the land.” As it is explained there: “Egypt was lower than the other nations,” and so forth. This circumstance awakened a great cry within created nature: why should Israel, called “the tribes of God,” be under the enslavement of a nation lower and more degraded than all the nations? This cry awakened the salvation even before its time. This is what we say: “In every generation they stand against us to destroy us, and the Holy One, blessed be He, saves us from their hand.” In every generation, the more the most lowly prevail and make the enslavement heavier upon Israel, this very circumstance brings the salvation nearer, awakening it even before its time. All this is because the blessed God constantly devises means that no one banished from Him remain banished, bringing salvation nearer even before the appointed time, before the full purpose of Israel’s clarifications has been completed. This is what that salvation, awakened through a question and a wonder, indicates. We therefore make changes at the Seder too, so that people will ask and answer: to teach that one must always establish a question and a cry within the heart, and through this salvation will be awakened even before its time.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim gives the cry generated by a question a specific role in redemption: it can awaken help even before all clarification has been completed. This illuminates the movement from felt poverty to full-hearted speech in Et HaOchel. The two accounts are not identical: Et HaOchel describes the soul’s expanding vitality, while Sod Yesharim explains why questioning and crying out matter within an unfinished process of redemption.

records.originEnglish: Maror is called in the language of the Mishnah an accompaniment to bread. As Tosafot write in the chapter Arvei Pesachim, it draws the heart toward food. So do all bitter, sharp, sour, and salty things, as we learned in the chapter “How Does One Bless?”: bread and a salty food draw the heart. Correspondingly, in the soul’s vitality they generate life and a desire to seek life. In the first chapter of Berakhot, they compared salt to suffering. Maror likewise recalls “They embittered their lives”; and as it is written, three good gifts come through suffering. So too in Egypt: “The more they afflicted it, the more it multiplied and spread”—with an increase of life.
