records.targetEnglish: “This maror that we eat,” and so forth, “because the Egyptians embittered our ancestors’ lives,” and so forth. The matter of maror is like what we find in the holy Zohar: “Had Israel not descended to Egypt and been refined there, they would not have been His unique people,” and so forth. To understand this: is it not written, “When the Most High allotted nations,” and so forth, “For God’s portion is His people”? Israel was already God’s portion from the generation of the Dispersion. The explanation is that Israel was God’s portion then too, but only from the side of the lot—that is, from the blessed God’s side. In Egypt, however, Israel clarified through the action of their service that they were God’s portion. This is “Had Israel not descended to Egypt,” and so forth. Through being in Egypt amid intense concealment, as it is written, “For you know how we dwelt in the land of Egypt ... and you saw their abominations and their idols,” and nevertheless having the strength to restrain themselves there, it became clarified that they were “Jacob, the cord of His inheritance.” Through their service they possess a line and a cord as the Holy One’s portion and lot, for through their service they recognize the line and cord by which they are connected to the root. As it is written, “To know that I am God who sanctifies you.” This recognition is possible only through the intense concealment that preceded it.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim specifies what can be gained through the bitterness before redemption: a bond first given from above becomes recognized through Israel’s own restrained service under concealment. This gives a distinct content to the increase of life described in Et HaOchel. The connection retains the role of service and recognition; it does not treat pain by itself as the completed good.

records.originEnglish: The fifth cup is optional according to the Rif. It appears to me that it corresponds to “I will bring you to the land.” This is why the Great Hallel is said over it on account of nourishment, which comes from the land, as we bless, “Who brings bread forth from the earth.” The inheritance of the land has not been completed in this world, since it was taken away, but will be in the future. Accordingly, at the beginning of the chapter Chelek, we say that all Israel has a share in the World to Come on the basis of the verse, “They will inherit the land forever.” The future inheritance of the land alludes to the World to Come. This is the meaning of “For His kindness is forever”: God’s kindness is everlasting, and they have a share in the World to Come even though it is not felt at present. Therefore this cannot be obligatory: to have joy in something not in one’s possession, clearly revealed before one’s eyes. It is not every person’s quality to be able to live from the inheritance of the land even though the land is not in our possession. In truth, “His kindness is forever,” and the bond has never been entirely severed. This is optional for one who merits it.
records.themeTitle: Joy in a promised inheritance depends on perceiving what remains concealed
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel explains the optional fifth cup through a future inheritance whose fulfillment is not presently visible. The promise can sustain joy, but the author does not presume that every person can yet live from that recognition.

records.targetEnglish: Therefore the fifth cup is optional; it cannot be established as an obligation. On the contrary, according to what the blessed God established as obligatory for human beings, nothing more is needed: when a person merits life, the inward meaning of chayah, he also merits complete union, the inward meaning of yechidah—the kisses of His mouth that are better than wine. It was not the blessed God’s will that a person sin and return in repentance at all. As it is written in Bereshit Rabbah on the verse “God saw that the light was good”: He chose the deeds of the righteous and not the deeds of the wicked—that is, after they have returned in repentance. Although, from the side of the world’s creation, it was “darkness first,” and light’s advantage comes from darkness, this is from the side of the corruptions in the world. From the side of the human being, who has a deficiency, he can attain a higher level through the greater filling of his lack, by the light that follows darkness. But from the blessed God’s side, He desires the good light. Therefore it is only optional, according to the person’s condition and his knowledge that his heart is still not entirely whole. Although every Israelite sees himself as though he left Egypt and merits the revelation of the Divine Presence that occurred then, in every generation on that night, nevertheless the abundance of impurity from the kinds of evil filling the heart’s hollow—from the leaven in the dough and the subjugation of exile, the thorns surrounding the rose—still stands around it. Even though the chametz has been removed for the moment from the inward depths of the heart, it has not been entirely removed from the world. It therefore prevents the revelation of the Divine Presence on Pesach night from becoming revealed within the heart; it remains concealed. The fifth cup is therefore needed to give the hidden root of life room to spread, so that life will also be sustained, through the addition of joy in the heart, by which the heart expands further. This is in the sense of “Your heart will fear and expand”: as fear of God increases in the heart, expansion and joy also increase within it. Through this, the hidden root of the source of his life, attached to the living God and King of the world, also spreads within the chambers of the heart until it becomes revealed, and sustenance following redemption is drawn forth.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz gives another account of the same optional cup and the concealed life that added joy can make felt. Its emphasis is nourishment after redemption and the heart’s incomplete reception of Divine life; Et HaOchel emphasizes the future inheritance. The comparison explains what the additional joy can accomplish without collapsing the two explanations or removing Machshavot Charutz’s explicit rejection of any claim that God desires sin followed by repentance.

records.originEnglish: The fifth cup is optional according to the Rif. It appears to me that it corresponds to “I will bring you to the land.” This is why the Great Hallel is said over it on account of nourishment, which comes from the land, as we bless, “Who brings bread forth from the earth.” The inheritance of the land has not been completed in this world, since it was taken away, but will be in the future. Accordingly, at the beginning of the chapter Chelek, we say that all Israel has a share in the World to Come on the basis of the verse, “They will inherit the land forever.” The future inheritance of the land alludes to the World to Come. This is the meaning of “For His kindness is forever”: God’s kindness is everlasting, and they have a share in the World to Come even though it is not felt at present. Therefore this cannot be obligatory: to have joy in something not in one’s possession, clearly revealed before one’s eyes. It is not every person’s quality to be able to live from the inheritance of the land even though the land is not in our possession. In truth, “His kindness is forever,” and the bond has never been entirely severed. This is optional for one who merits it.
records.themeTitle: Joy in a promised inheritance depends on perceiving what remains concealed
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel explains the optional fifth cup through a future inheritance whose fulfillment is not presently visible. The promise can sustain joy, but the author does not presume that every person can yet live from that recognition.
records.targetHebrew: ולזה נקרא נמי זה החג זמן שמחתינו כי כיון שישראל מחזירין הכל לההתחלה להשם אהיה דאנא זמין לאולדא מחמת זה נתרבה השמחה וע"ד מאמרם ז"ל (מדרש שמיני ובגמ' מגילה) אין והיה אלא שמחה וכו' כי והיה רומז על זה שלא מסר עדיין השי"ת לידו של אדם רק שזמין ליתן ומאחר שהוא עדיין בבחינת דאנא זמין לאולדא וגבי השי"ת יש עד אין שיעור ליתן עד בלי גבול. אבל ויהי איתא במדרש (שם) אין ויהי אלא לשון צער כי ויהי מורה שכבר הוא ביד האדם ומה שבא ברשות אדם נתיישן והטובה הוא בצמצום הגבול ועלול להפסד.
records.targetEnglish: This is also why this festival is called “the season of our joy.” Since Israel returns everything to the beginning, to the name Ehyeh—“I am ready to bring forth”—joy increases through this. It follows the Sages’ statement in Midrash Shemini and in Megillah: “Ve-hayah is only an expression of joy.” For ve-hayah indicates what the blessed God has not yet placed in a person’s hands, but is ready to give. Since it is still in the state of “I am ready to bring forth,” there is no measure to what the blessed God has to give, without limit. But concerning va-yehi, the Midrash says there: “Va-yehi is only an expression of sorrow.” Va-yehi indicates what is already in the person’s hands. What has come into human possession grows old; the good is confined within a boundary and is liable to loss.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains how what has not yet entered one’s possession can itself sustain joy: the future Divine gift is not confined to the limits of the good already held. This illuminates the recognition needed for Et HaOchel’s joy in the still-unfulfilled inheritance. Sod Yesharim does not discuss the fifth cup or its legal status; the optionality and its limit remain Et HaOchel’s own argument.

records.originEnglish: The inward meaning of the first dipping, karpas, is known from the Ari: it alludes to the consciousness of smallness. Its meaning corresponds to what our Sages said: “So that the children will notice and ask.” Questioning is attributed to children and the small, because smallness entails a lack of knowledge. Nevertheless, it is some knowledge, and one needs the consciousness of smallness in order to recognize what to ask. The Sages established this from Scripture’s wording, “When your son asks you,” and so forth: the telling of the Exodus proceeds through questions and answers, and a person asks himself. This is the order of receiving light on this night: through the question one receives the answer, and through the prior smallness the greatness afterward shines within him.
records.themeTitle: The capacity to ask is already a beginning of understanding
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel distinguishes having no understanding from having enough understanding to recognize a question. The Seder deliberately awakens that first capacity, through which a fuller answer can subsequently be received.

records.targetHebrew: ושאינו יודע לשאול את פתח לו. היינו כמו שאמר אאמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה אשר מי שלומד דברי תורה ואינו קשה לו בהם שום קושיא זהו סימן מובהק שלא נגע עדיין בדברי תורה כי מאחר שהשכל של דברי תורה הוא באמת להיפך מהשכל של זה העולם וא"כ מהיכן ישר בעיניו כ"כ ולא קשה לו שום קושיא אלא בטח לפי שלא נגע עדיין בהם. אולם מי שקשה לו בד"ת ומייגע א"ע אח"כ לתרץ זאת הוא ד"ת ולכן מי שאינו יודע לשאול ואינו קשה לו כלום זה בטח לא נגע עדיין בדברי תורה לזה את פתח לו היינו שצריכין להשתדל עמו ולפתוח לו דרך שיהי' ג"כ יכול לשאול ולתרץ ולזה אמרו ז"ל בגמ' לעשות פעולות במכוון כדי שישאלו התנוקות היינו למען שיהי' חידש בעיני הרואים ויקשה כגון חוטפין מצה מלפני התנוקות כדי שישאלו:
records.targetEnglish: “As for one who does not know how to ask, you open for him.” This is as my holy father and teacher, of blessed memory, said: someone who learns words of Torah and has no difficulty in them at all shows a clear sign that he has not yet touched words of Torah. Since the understanding of Torah is in truth the opposite of this world’s understanding, how could it seem so straightforward to him, with no difficulty at all? Surely it is because he has not yet touched it. But someone who has difficulty in words of Torah and then exerts himself to resolve it—that is words of Torah. Therefore, one who does not know how to ask and finds nothing difficult has certainly not yet touched words of Torah. Thus “you open for him”: one must work with him and open a path so that he too can ask and answer. This is why the Sages said in the Gemara to perform actions deliberately so that the children will ask—that is, so that there will be something new in the observers’ eyes that presents a difficulty, such as snatching the matzah away from the children so that they will ask.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim explains why an absence of questions need not indicate understanding. A question can mark the learner’s first real encounter with a form of understanding different from what he already assumes. Its instruction to open a path for the child gives practical content to the initial consciousness that Et HaOchel says the Seder must awaken.

records.originEnglish: In non-leap years, after Pesach we read the portion Shemini, in which it says, “These are the living creatures that you may eat,” and so forth; this passage too teaches setting boundaries in matters of eating. Through the holiness of eating matzah, one afterward merits clarifying the evil within eating. In every matter, through first becoming sanctified with its particular holiness, one afterward merits clarifying the evil—like “I am,” followed by “You shall have no,” and so forth. Likewise, the portion Shemini itself begins with Aaron’s selection as High Priest and the holiness of the priests. Our Sages expounded in Vayikra Rabbah: “‘From the eater came food’—this is Aaron the priest, who eats all the offerings.” Aaron is simply called “the eater,” for this is the essence of priestly holiness: the holiness of eating, so that all his food comes from the table of the Most High and the remainders of sacred offerings. Through this, the portion concludes with clarifying the evil in eating: “These are the living creatures,” and so forth, ending, “To distinguish between the impure and the pure, and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.”
records.themeTitle: Receiving holiness makes the subsequent discrimination possible
records.themeSummary: Et HaOchel reads the sequence from matzah to Shemini, and from priestly eating to permitted species, through “I am” before “You shall have no.” A received positive holiness supplies the basis for the later work of distinction.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Bo 5
records.targetHebrew: הָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה כִּי חֻקַּת הַפֶּסַח הוּא נֶגֶד דִּבֵּר "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֶיךָ" שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל מִצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה, וְחֻקַּת הַפָּרָה הוּא נֶגֶד "לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ" שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וּבֶאֱמֶת מֵהָרָאוּי עַל פִּי שֵׂכֶל, שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל הָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג יִקְרַת הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֶיךָ" קֹדֶם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִבּוֹ מְזֻכָּךְ מִ"לֹּא יִהְיֶה לְךָ", כִּי תְּחִלָּה צָרִיךְ הָאָדָם לָסוּר מֵרָע וְאַחַר כָּךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת טוֹב, אַךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרֹב רַחֲמָיו הִקְדִּים מַאֲמַר "אָנֹכִי" קֹדֶם "לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ", כִּי בְּאִם לָאו לֹא הָיָה אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁיָּכוֹל לָבוֹא לְהַשִּׂיג דִּבּוּר "אָנֹכִי", כִּי מִי הוּא הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַר זִכִּיתִי לִבִּי בְּכָל מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וְעַל זֶה אָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (תְּהִלִּים קוּף לָמֶד חֵית, בֵּית) "כִּי הִגְדַּלְתָּ עַל כָּל שִׁמְךָ אִמְרָתֶךָ", וַאֲמִירָה הַיְנוּ בִּלְחִישָׁה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יְבָרֵר אַחַר כָּךְ כִּי לֵב יִשְׂרָאֵל מְנֻקֶּה. וְעַל זֶה אָמַר "אוֹדֶה שִׁמְךָ" הַיְנוּ הַטּוֹבָה וְהַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ עִמָּנוּ לָתֵת לָנוּ תְּחִלָּה דִּבֵּר "אָנֹכִי", כְּדֵי שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ יְבָרֵר בְּלִבֵּנוּ הַדִּבּוּר "לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ",
records.targetEnglish: The matter is that the statute of the Passover offering corresponds to the utterance “I am the Lord your God,” which includes all the positive commandments, while the statute of the red heifer corresponds to “You shall have no,” which includes all the prohibitions. In truth, according to reason, it would be fitting that a person could not attain the preciousness of “I am the Lord your God” before his heart had been purified of “You shall have no,” for a person must first turn from evil and afterward do good. But the blessed God, in His abundant mercy, placed “I am” before “You shall have no.” Otherwise there would be no person in the world able to attain the utterance “I am,” for who could say, “I have purified my heart” regarding all the prohibitions? Concerning this King David, peace be upon him, said, “For You have magnified Your utterance beyond all Your name.” An utterance means a whisper: the blessed God will afterward clarify that Israel’s heart is clean. Concerning this he said, “I will thank Your name”—the goodness and greatness You have done for us by first giving us the utterance “I am,” so that afterward the utterance “You shall have no” will be clarified in our hearts.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains why the positive gift must precede complete purification. If recognition of “I am” were withheld until every prohibition had already been fully clarified, no one could begin. This supplies the reason behind Et HaOchel’s sequence: the holiness first received through the mitzvah enables the subsequent work of distinguishing what may be received from what must be rejected.
